source_text: Ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ τοῖς γεγαμηκόσι παραινέσαιμι ἂν οἴκοι τὰς γυναῖκας τὰς σφῶν μήποτε κατὰ πρόσωπον οἰκετῶν φιλεῖν. οὐδὲ γὰρ προσγελᾶν δούλοις Ἀριστοτέλης εἴα ποτέ, πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ κατ᾿ ὄψιν αὐτῶν φιλοφρονούμενον φαίνεσθαι τὴν γυναῖκα. ἄμεινον δὲ οἴκοθεν ἀρξαμένους ἀπὸ τοῦ γάμου τὴν σεμνότητα ἐπιδείκνυσθαι. μεγίστη γὰρ ἡ σωφροσύνης συζυγία καθαρᾶς ἡδονῆς ἀποπνέουσα. πάνυ γοῦν θαυμασίως ἡ τραγῳδία. φεῦ φεῦ, γυναῖκες, (φησίν) ὡς ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἄρα οὐ χρυσός, οὐ τυραννίς, οὐ πλούτου χλιδὴ τοσοῦτον εἶχε διαφόρους τὰς ἡδονὰς ὡς ἀνδρὸς ἐσθλοῦ καὶ γυναικὸς εὐσεβοῦς γνώμη δικαία καὶ φρονοῦσα τἄνδικα. ταῦτα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τὰ παραγγέλματα καὶ παρὰ τοῖς τὴν κοσμικὴν μετιοῦσι σοφίαν ἐκφωνηθέντα οὐ παραιτητέον. ἐγνωκότες οὖν »τὸ ἑκάστου ἔργον, ἐν φόβῳ τὸν τῆς παροικίας ὑμῶν χρόνον ἀναστράφητε, εἰδότες ὅτι οὐ φθαρτοῖς, ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ, ἐλυτρώθημεν ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ἡμῶν ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου, ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι ὡς ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου Χριστοῦ.« »ἀρκετὸς οὖν ὁ παρεληλυθὼς χρόνος,« ὁ Πέτρος φησί, »τὸ βούλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατειργάσθαι, πεπορευμένους ἐν ἀσελγείαις, ἐπιθυμίαις, οἰνοφλυγίαις, κώμοις, πότοις καὶ ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις.« ὅρον ἔχωμεν τὸν σταυρὸν τοῦ κυρίου, ᾧ περισταυρούμεθα καὶ περιθριγκούμεθα τῶν προτέρων ἁμαρτιῶν. ἀναγεννηθέντες τοίνυν προσηλωθῶμεν [ἐν] τῇ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀνανήψωμέν τε καὶ ἁγιασθῶμεν, »ὅτι οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ὦτα αὐτοῦ εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν, πρόσωπον δὲ κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακά. καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ἡμᾶς, ἐὰν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ζηλωταὶ γενώμεθα;« ἡ δὲ ἀρίστη ἀγωγὴ εὐταξία ἐστίν, παντελὴς οὖσα εὐσχημοσύνη καὶ δύναμις τεταγμένη βεβαία, τῶν ἑξῆς ἀλλήλοις κειμένων ἐν ἔργῳ καλῶς ἀποδοτική, κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἀνυπέρβλητος. Ταῦτα, εἰ καὶ τραχύτερον προηνέχθην οἰκονομούμενος τῆς ἐπανορθώσεως τὴν σωτηρίαν, ἐμοὶ μὲν λελέχθων, φησὶν ὁ παιδαγωγός, ἐπειδὴ »ὁ ἐλέγχων μετὰ παρρησίας εἰρηνοποιεῖ,« ὑμεῖς δὲ εἰ μὲν ἀκούσεσθέ μου, σωθήσεσθε, εἰ δ᾿ οὐ προσέξετε τοῖς εἰρημένοις, οὔ μοι μέλει· μέλει δὲ ὅμως καὶ οὕτως· »τὴν γὰρ μετάνοιαν τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ μᾶλλον ἢ τὸν θάνατον αἱρεῖται.« »ἢν δὲ εἰσακούσητέ μου, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε«, ὁ παιδαγωγὸς πάλιν λέγει, γῆς ἀγαθὰ τὰ ἀνθρώπεια ὀνομάζων καλά, τὸ κάλλος, τὸν πλοῦτον, τὴν ὑγίειαν καὶ τὴν ἰσχύν, τὴν τροφήν· ἀγαθὰ μὲν γὰρ ὄντως »ἃ οὔτε οὖς ἤκουσεν οὔτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνέβη ποτέ«, περὶ τὸν ὄντως ὄντα βασιλέα τὰ ὄντως ὄντα ἀγαθὰ ὄντα καὶ ἀναμένοντα ἡμᾶς· ἀγαθῶν γάρ ἐστι καὶ δοτὴρ καὶ φύλαξ· κατὰ μετουσίαν δὲ ἐκείνων τὰ τῇδε συνωνυμεῖ, παιδαγωγοῦντος ἐνθέως τοῦ λόγου τὴν ἀνθρώπων ἀσθένειαν ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐπὶ τὴν νόησιν.
pass_a_gloss: But I would also advise those who are married to love their own wives at home, not in the presence of servants. For neither does Aristotle ever allow slaves to be fondled, and it is necessary for the wife to appear to be affectionate towards them in their presence. But it is better for those who have begun at home from marriage to show dignity. For the greatest marriage is that of chastity, breathing pure pleasure. The tragedy says, 'Alas, alas, women,' (it says) that among humans, neither gold nor tyranny nor the abundance of wealth has as many different pleasures as the opinion of a good man and a pious woman, a just and manly-minded opinion. These are the commands of righteousness, and they have been proclaimed not only by those who possess worldly wisdom, and they should not be rejected. Having known, therefore, 'each one's work, conduct your time of sojourning in fear, knowing that you were not redeemed from your vain conversation, handed down from your fathers, with corruptible things, silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and spotless, Christ.' 'The past time is enough,' Peter says, 'to have done the will of the Gentiles, having walked in lasciviousness, lusts, wine-drinkings, revelings, drinking parties, and unlawful idolatries.' Let us have the cross of the Lord as our limit, by which we are crucified and put to death to our former sins. Having been reborn, therefore, let us be devoted to the truth and let us be raised and sanctified, 'for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are open to their prayers, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. And who will harm us if we become zealous for what is good?' But the best guidance is self-control, being complete modesty and steadfast power, with the things that follow being well-ordered and placed in action, unbeaten in virtue. These things, even if they were spoken more roughly, being managed for the sake of correction and salvation, 'for he who rebukes with boldness makes peace,' the Pedagogue says. If you listen to me, you will be saved, but if you do not pay attention to what has been said, I do not care; yet I do care: 'for repentance of the sinner is chosen rather than death.' 'But if you listen to me, you will eat the good things of the earth,' the Pedagogue says again, calling human goods 'good things,' beauty, wealth, health, and strength, nourishment. For the things that 'neither ear has heard nor has arisen in the heart' are indeed good, concerning the truly existing King, the truly existing good things that are waiting for us. For He is the giver and guardian of good things; but the things that are named after them here are used by metonymy, the Word guiding human weakness from the senses to the intellect.

pass_b_english: I would also advise married men to show affection to their own wives at home, not in the presence of servants. For Aristotle does not even permit slaves to be fondled; how much more necessary is it that a wife should appear affectionate toward them when they are watching. It is better to begin at home, from marriage itself, and to display dignity. For the greatest marriage is that of chastity, breathing pure pleasure. The tragedy puts it wonderfully: 'Alas, alas, women,' it says, 'among humans neither gold nor tyranny nor the abundance of wealth provides such varied pleasures as the judgment of a good man and a pious woman, a just and manly-minded judgment.' These are the commands of righteousness, and they have been proclaimed even among those who possess worldly wisdom; they must not be rejected. Since you know 'each one's work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourn, knowing that you were not redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your ancestors with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot' (1 Peter 1:17-19). 'The time that is past is enough,' Peter says, 'for doing the will of the Gentiles, living in licentiousness, passions, drunkenness, revels, carousing, and lawless idolatry' (1 Peter 4:3). Let us make the cross of the Lord our boundary, by which we are crucified and put to death to our former sins. Having been born again, therefore, let us cleave to the truth, let us be sobered and sanctified: 'for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. And who will harm you if you are zealous for what is good?' (1 Peter 3:12-13). But the best guidance is self-control, which is complete propriety and steadfast power, ordering the things that follow one another and rendering them well in action, unsurpassed in virtue. These things, even if I have spoken them somewhat roughly while managing the correction that leads to salvation — 'for he who rebukes with boldness makes peace,' the Pedagogue says — if you listen to me, you will be saved; but if you do not pay attention to what has been said, I do not care — yet I do care even so: 'for he chooses the repentance of the sinner rather than his death.' 'And if you listen to me, you will eat the good things of the earth,' the Pedagogue says again, calling human goods 'good things' — beauty, wealth, health, strength, nourishment. For the things that 'neither ear has heard nor has entered the heart of man' are truly good, concerning the truly existing King — the truly existing good things that exist and await us. For He is both the giver and the guardian of good things; but the things here that share their names do so by metonymy, the Word guiding human weakness from the senses to the intellect.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text, including the nuances of the Pedagogue's rhetorical style and the metonymy at the end. Scripture citations in Pass B (1 Peter 1:17-19, 1 Peter 4:3, 1 Peter 3:12-13) correctly identify the source of the quoted/alluded clauses. Pass A and B are consistent with the Greek and each other.
